abstract: 1.) Nectar is a crucial resource for a wide range of insect species and one of the driving forces shaping plant-pollinator interactions. Flowers have evolved diverse strategies to restrict nectar access, ensuring only beneficial flower visits resulting in successful pollination. This range of adaptations, often morphological, makes it difficult for researchers to collect nectar in a standardised manner. In this study, we compare common methods used for nectar extraction, with a focus on applicability across several plant families 2.) We assessed pre-treatment methods widely used before nectar extraction, such as pollinator exclusion by bagging flowers, storing flowers overnight in water, and standing nectar crop (unmanipulated control). Moreover, we compared the effectiveness of two commonly used nectar extraction techniques, i.e., centrifugation and microcapillaries, across a range of flower morphologies. We compared nectar volume, sugar concentration, and total sugar content obtained by different methods for 23 flower species from 16 plant families. 3) We show that pollinator exclusion by bagging is an effective measure to obtain maximum nectar volume regardless of plant growth type. The nectar sugar concentration of herbaceous and woody species showed pre-treatment specific variation. Extraction with a centrifuge consistently yielded more nectar volume without altering the sugar concentration, while microcapillary extraction was not effective for most flower morphologies, especially lip (e.g. Salvia pratensis) and disc-shaped flowers (e.g. Rosa canina). 4.) Our results provide a foundation for the standardisation of floral nectar extraction protocols, improving comparability across studies, and facilitating broader ecological and evolutionary research that depends on consistent and reliable nectar sampling.
